title: When spam messages bypass Discord's built-in AutoMod, I want to automatically detect and remove them
job_to_be_done: When spam messages bypass Discord's built-in AutoMod, I want to automatically detect and remove them using custom regex filters, so I can protect community trust and reduce moderator workload.
painful_workflow: Manually reviewing and removing spam messages that bypass Discord's built-in AutoMod, using third-party bots or manual deletion.
current_workaround: Use third-party moderation bots with custom regex filters (e.g., Dyno, Carl-bot) or manually delete messages and ban users.
verified_facts: SIG-0002 (from SRC-0002, a Discord forum post collected 2025-04-10) reports that spam messages bypass Discord's built-in AutoMod, including repeated links and scam messages using character manipulation.
SIG-0002 states the current workaround is third-party moderation bots with custom regex filters (Dyno, Carl-bot) or manual deletion and banning.
SIG-0002 claims the problem occurs daily in high-traffic servers.
The cluster is supported by exactly one independent source and one source type.
inferences: Because free, mature bots (Dyno, Carl-bot) already provide the exact capability described in the JTBD (custom regex spam filtering), the unmet headroom for a new paid product is likely small.
The target user base (volunteer Discord moderators/admins) likely has little to no budget authority, suppressing willingness to pay even where pain exists.
The residual pain is concentrated in edge cases that existing bots miss (e.g., character-manipulation scams), which is a narrower problem than the cluster framing suggests.
assumptions: The single forum signal is assumed to be representative of a broader moderator population, which is unverified.
The claim of daily frequency in high-traffic servers is taken at face value from one source without corroboration.
It is assumed that Discord's native AutoMod has not since closed the regex/filtering gap, which would further shrink the opportunity.
unknowns: Whether existing bots (Dyno, Carl-bot) actually fail in ways users would pay to fix, and how often.
Whether any server admins currently pay for moderation tooling, and how much.
The size of the segment of high-traffic, commercially motivated servers (e.g., brand/community servers with revenue at stake) versus volunteer hobby servers.
Whether scam-driven member harm translates into measurable churn or revenue loss for server owners.
Whether Discord's own AutoMod roadmap (keyword/wildcard/filter improvements) eliminates the gap natively.
